newsitem.title: COMOROS: More bodies pulled from downed Ethiopian plane.
newsitem.headline: More bodies pulled from downed Ethiopian plane.

text.p: A section of the Ethiopian Airlines plane which crashed on Saturday off the Comoro Islands was winched onto a beach on Monday with bodies still dangling from buckled seats.
A section of the Boeing 767, which ran out of fuel and ditched into the sea killing 123 people, was dragged ashore from the spot some 500 metres (yards) off the beach where it crashed.

The plane was hijacked by three men, believed to be Ethiopians, en route to Nairobi and West Africa from Addis Ababa. Fifty-two of the 175 passengers and crew survived, including two of the suspected hijackers.

Ethiopian Airlines, Africa's flag-ship carrier, made preparations on Monday for a mass repatriation of the victims to the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa, but their efforts were hindered by a lack of coffins on the Moslem island-chain.

"The problem we have is that we have no coffins in the Comoros. We are a Moslem country. Possibly Ethiopian Airlines may bring some in," the Commander of the Comoran gendarmerie, Ismael Mognidaho, told Reuters.
Moslems bury their dead in shrouds instead of coffins and cremation is not allowed.
Mognidaho said the authorities of the islands, lying in the Indian Ocean 300 km (190 miles) east of the African mainland, had no problem in principle with a mass repatriation.
Airline officials believe it will be easier for relatives to go to the Ethiopian capital than to the Comoros to identify their kin and make arrangements for the bodies.
A special plane to transport the victims was not expected to arrive in the Comoros until Wednesday.
India's honorary consul in the Comoros had asked if Hindus could be cremated immediately, in line with the religion, but the request had been turned down.

Lia Belai, the public relations head of the airline, said that after proper identifications and prayer services in Addis Ababa, the bodies would be transported to their respective destinations accompanied by airline officials.
She said the airline would make arrangements for those who wished to take the body of a relative direct from the Comoros.
Of the 163 passengers and 12 crew on board the plane, 145 were international travellers from some 35 countries and 30 were Ethiopians.

The bodies that have been found are being kept in a makeshift morgue in what used to be the cold storage facilities of a meat importer. By early Monday only two families had arrived on the island to try to identify relatives.
Ethiopian Airlines said it would not be issuing a passenger list "until proper identifications were carried out and the next of kin was informed", Lia said.
Ethiopia has declared a three-day mourning period starting on Monday and flags are flying at half-mast.
The national radio played solemn music and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church said it would hold a requiem mass on Tuesday for all those who died in the crash.

The United States Embassy in Addis Ababa condemned what it called the "criminal and terrorist act" and said the Federal Bureau of Investigation would enter the investigation because U.S. citizens had been on the flight.
Airline sources said a team of 18 Israelis had identified the bodies of three countrymen, but a dispute with the Comoron authorities had prevented them leaving the islands.
The authorities say they were only allowed into the country on condition they remained and helped also identify non-Israeli victims. A team from South Africa, meanwhile, were denied entry permission.

The Comoran police were using hacksaws and anything else that came to hand to break into the wreck. They pulled out one more body on Monday morning, that of a woman in shorts, still clutching a small, black rucksack.
Police said some bodies remained inside the front section of the plane which, with the cockpit, was under water and unlikely to be salvaged immediately.
The back of the plane was also still in the sea, the green bit of the green-red-and-yellow tail visible above the water.
